title: Filtering groups
objectives: Explain why `WHERE` cannot test an aggregate
Combine `WHERE` and `HAVING` and sort groups by an aggregate

screens.title: Busy tickers
screens.prose: One day of fills for three tickers. Risk wants the tickers that traded more than three times.
screens.question: Tap the ticker cell of every fill in a ticker with more than 3 fills.

hints.text: Count the fills of each ticker first.
AZN, BARC and SHEL appear 4, 3 and 2 times.
Only AZN has more than 3. Tap its four ticker cells.

feedback.correct: AZN has 4 fills; BARC has 3 and SHEL 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each ticker, then keep those with 4 or more.

byKey.with-barc: You included BARC, which has exactly 3 fills. More than 3 means 4 or more.
byKey.r1c1: BARC has exactly 3 fills, which is not more than 3.

explain.text: You counted each ticker's fills, then kept the tickers whose count passed. The test applied to whole groups, not to single rows.

screens.title: Can WHERE do it?
screens.prose:
A first attempt puts the count test in `WHERE`.

```sql
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*)
FROM trades
WHERE COUNT(*) > 3
GROUP BY ticker;
```
screens.question: What does SQLite do with this query?

options.why: You read `WHERE` as a test on each group. It runs on single rows, before any group exists.
You expected SQLite to skip the test it cannot use. It refuses the query instead.

hints.text: When does `WHERE` run: before or after `GROUP BY`?
`WHERE` looks at one row at a time.
A single row has no count of fills, so the test cannot be evaluated.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what `COUNT(*)` means for one row on its own.

explain.text: `WHERE` tests one row at a time, before any group exists. A lone row has no count, so SQLite stops with `misuse of aggregate: COUNT()`.

canvas.caption: WHERE sees one row: no count yet

screens.title: A filter for groups
screens.prose:
The fix moves the test after the grouping.

```sql
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*)
FROM trades
GROUP BY ticker
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
```
screens.question: What does this return?

options.why: You kept BARC, which has exactly 3. `> 3` lets through only 4 or more.
You ignored the last line. It removes every group whose count fails the test.

hints.text: Form the three groups first, then test each count.
The counts are 4, 3 and 2.
Only a count of 4 is more than 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each group's count against `> 3`.

explain.text: `HAVING` is `WHERE` for groups: it runs after `GROUP BY`, so it can test an aggregate. Only AZN's count of 4 passes, exactly as you did by hand.

screens.title: Both filters
screens.prose:
```sql
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*)
FROM trades
WHERE qty >= 300
GROUP BY ticker
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
```
screens.question: How many rows does this return?

hints.text: Apply `WHERE` to the fills before you count anything.
Fills of 300 or more: one AZN, three BARC, two SHEL.
Counts after `WHERE` are 1, 3 and 2. Keep those of at least 2.

feedback.correct: BARC and SHEL pass; AZN is left with one fill.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Filter the fills, then group, then test the counts.

byKey.having-first: You counted AZN's four fills. `WHERE` drops its fills under 300 shares first, leaving one, so AZN fails.
byKey.one: SHEL has two fills of 300 or more, and `>= 2` includes 2.

explain.text: `WHERE` keeps fills of 300 shares or more, so AZN keeps only its 500. Grouping gives counts of 1, 3 and 2, and `HAVING` keeps BARC and SHEL.

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

db.executemany("INSERT INTO trades VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    (1, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 200, 118.90),
    (2, "2024-03-12", "BARC", 5000, 2.17),
    (3, "2024-03-12", "SHEL", 300, 26.00),
    (4, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 500, 119.20),
    (5, "2024-03-12", "BARC", 8000, 2.19),
    (6, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 100, 119.00),
    (7, "2024-03-12", "SHEL", 400, 26.05),
    (8, "2024-03-12", "BARC", 3000, 2.18),
    (9, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 150, 119.10),
])


def query():
    return """
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*), SUM(qty)
FROM trades
GROUP BY ticker
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY ticker
"""

screens.title: Filtering too early
screens.prose: Risk asks for the tickers whose **average** fill is above 250 shares, with that average.
screens.question: Which query answers it?

options.why: You filtered the fills before averaging. AZN's small fills vanish, so its average jumps from 237.5 to 500 and it slips in.

canvas.caption: WHERE kept only AZN's 500: its average jumps to 500

options.why: `WHERE` runs before the groups exist, so there is no average to test. SQLite stops with an error.

hints.text: Which average does Risk mean: of all fills, or of the large ones?
AZN averages 237.5 shares over all four fills.
The test must run on the finished average, after grouping.

feedback.correct: BARC and SHEL qualify; AZN averages 237.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The test is on each ticker's average over all its fills.

byKey.where: You filtered the fills before averaging. AZN's small fills vanish, so its average jumps from 237.5 to 500 and it slips in.

explain.text: A `WHERE` on `qty` changes which fills enter each average, so it changes the averages themselves. `HAVING` leaves the averages alone and only drops groups: AZN at 237.5 goes.

screens.title: The order SQL works in
screens.prose: We have seen `WHERE` run before groups exist and `HAVING` run after. Put every step of a grouped query in the order the database carries it out.
screens.question: Order the steps, first to last.

lines.text: `WHERE`: drop single rows that fail a row test
`GROUP BY`: pile the surviving rows into groups
`HAVING`: drop groups that fail an aggregate test
`SELECT`: compute one output row per group

hints.text: A step can only use what the step before it produced.
`HAVING` needs groups, so it comes after `GROUP BY`.
Rows, row filter, groups, group filter, output, sort.

feedback.correct: Rows, row filter, groups, group filter, output, sort.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the result of the one before it.

explain.text: `WHERE` sees rows, so it comes before grouping; `HAVING` sees groups, so it comes after. `ORDER BY` sorts finished rows, which is why it can sort by an aggregate.

screens.title: Two filters, two jobs
screens.prose:
A row test goes in `WHERE`; a test on an aggregate goes in `HAVING`.

```sql
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*)   -- 5. one row per group
FROM trades               -- 1. every row
WHERE qty >= 300          -- 2. drop rows
GROUP BY ticker           -- 3. form groups
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2      -- 4. drop groups
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;   -- 6. sort the result
```
screens.question: Which condition can only go in `HAVING`?

options.why: That tests a single fill, so it belongs in `WHERE`. In `HAVING`, a bare `qty` would test one arbitrary fill per group.
`WHERE` can test each row's ticker. Doing it there also saves grouping rows you will throw away.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the test that needs a whole group to evaluate.

explain.text: `SUM(qty)` exists only once rows are grouped, so it must be tested in `HAVING`. Tests on single columns belong in `WHERE`.

screens.title: A liquid universe
screens.prose: A strategy should trade only names with plenty of activity. The starter generates a day of fills: 24 for AZN, 31 for BARC, 20 for SHEL and 12 for HSBA.

state.caption: fills per ticker in the generated table

screens.question: Return each ticker with more than 20 fills and its count, most active first.

widget.starter:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE trades(id INTEGER, date TEXT, ticker TEXT, qty INTEGER, price REAL)")
base = {"AZN": 118.90, "BARC": 2.17, "SHEL": 26.00, "HSBA": 6.45}
counts = {"AZN": 24, "BARC": 31, "SHEL": 20, "HSBA": 12}
n = 0
for ticker in counts:
    for k in range(counts[ticker]):
        n += 1
        db.execute("INSERT INTO trades VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                   (n, "2024-03-12", ticker, 100 * (k % 5 + 1), base[ticker]))


def query():
    return """
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*)
FROM trades
GROUP BY ticker
"""
widget.solution:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE trades(id INTEGER, date TEXT, ticker TEXT, qty INTEGER, price REAL)")
base = {"AZN": 118.90, "BARC": 2.17, "SHEL": 26.00, "HSBA": 6.45}
counts = {"AZN": 24, "BARC": 31, "SHEL": 20, "HSBA": 12}
n = 0
for ticker in counts:
    for k in range(counts[ticker]):
        n += 1
        db.execute("INSERT INTO trades VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                   (n, "2024-03-12", ticker, 100 * (k % 5 + 1), base[ticker]))


def query():
    return """
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*)
FROM trades
GROUP BY ticker
HAVING COUNT(*) > 20
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC
"""

hints.text: Count per ticker, keep the big counts, then sort.
`HAVING COUNT(*) > 20`, then `ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`.
`SELECT ticker, COUNT(*) FROM trades GROUP BY ticker HAVING COUNT(*) > 20 ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`

feedback.correct: BARC and AZN make the cut; SHEL's 20 is not more than 20.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the examples and compare your rows with the expected ones.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[('BARC', 31), ('AZN', 24)]`. Check the boundary and the sort direction.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 gives SHEL 21 fills, so SHEL must now appear, last.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 lifts AZN to 34 fills, so AZN must now come first. Sort by the count, not by name.

explain.text: `HAVING` drops the groups with 20 fills or fewer, so SHEL sits exactly on the line and is out. `ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC` then sorts the surviving groups by their own aggregate.

ideas: `WHERE` filters single rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters whole groups after it.
A test on an aggregate such as `COUNT(*)` or `AVG(qty)` can only go in `HAVING`.
The database works `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `SELECT`, then `ORDER BY`, so `ORDER BY` can sort by an aggregate.

formula.name: The order of work
formula.note: Rows are filtered before groups exist; groups are filtered after.

summary.trap: Moving a group test into `WHERE` changes which rows enter each average, so the averages themselves change.
